title: Looping words, not just numbers
idea: A list can hold strings; for-item-in-list visits each word the same way. Reviews strings and f-strings.

exercises.prompt:
names = ["Ada", "Lin", "Sam"]
for name in names:
    print(name)

What is printed?
options: Ada, Lin, Sam — each on its own line
exercises.explanation: The loop works the same for words: each string is handed to 'name' in turn and printed.

exercises.prompt:
names = ["Ada", "Lin"]
for name in names:
    print(f"Hi {name}!")

What shows?
exercises.explanation: The f-string drops each current word in for {name}, greeting every person.

exercises.prompt: The 'for item in list' tool only works on lists of numbers.
exercises.explanation: It visits each value whatever the type — numbers, words, anything in the list.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the code to greet each guest in a list of names.
exercises.explanation: List of names, loop header, indented greeting. Prints 'Welcome, Mo' then 'Welcome, Jo'.

exercises.prompt:
Greet each name. Fill the keyword:

names = ["Ada", "Lin"]
for name ____ names:
    print(name)
exercises.explanation: Same shape as always: 'for name in names:'. The 'in' keyword connects the variable to the list.
String comparison with == checks each word; only 'dog' matches, so the message prints once.

exercises.prompt:
colors = ["red", "blue"]
for color in colors:
    print("Color:", color)

Which line shows the loop visiting the SECOND item?
exercises.explanation: Second pass holds 'blue', so the line is 'Color: blue'.

exercises.prompt: A loop variable can hold a word on one pass and the next word on the next pass.
exercises.explanation: Each pass it takes the next value from the list — words here — one at a time.

exercises.prompt:
pets = ["cat", "dog"]
for pet in pets:
    print(pet + "!")

What shows?
exercises.explanation: Concatenation glues '!' to each word: 'cat!' then 'dog!'.

exercises.prompt: Big idea so far: 'for item in list' lets you...
options: Visit each value and act on it, numbers or words
exercises.explanation: It's the general 'do something to every value' tool — the type of the values doesn't matter.
